name: Aims, Hypotheses and Ethics
what: This subtopic covers how to write well-formed aims and hypotheses, how to distinguish between them, and how to evaluate the health, safety and ethical considerations relevant to a practical investigation.
why: Clear aims and hypotheses focus an investigation and allow results to be evaluated against predictions. Addressing safety and ethics is a VCE requirement and reflects responsible scientific practice.

items.title: I can distinguish between an aim and a hypothesis
items.what: An aim states the main purpose of an investigation — what it intends to find out. A hypothesis is a testable prediction of the expected outcome, based on existing theory, that can be supported or refuted by experimental results.
items.why: Confusing these two terms is a common error in VCE reports. An aim does not predict an outcome; a hypothesis does. Both are needed and serve different functions in structuring an investigation.
items.example: Aim: 'To determine whether the presence of the enzyme invertase increases the rate of hydrolysis of sucrose.' Hypothesis: 'The presence of invertase will increase the rate of hydrolysis of sucrose, producing a higher concentration of glucose, because invertase lowers the activation energy of the reaction.'

items.title: I can write a specific aim that references the independent and dependent variables
items.what: A well-written aim explicitly names both the independent and dependent variables and uses precise language. It should be a single, clear statement of what the investigation intends to measure or determine.
items.why: A vague aim makes it difficult to design a focused method and to evaluate results against the purpose of the investigation. Explicit variable reference also helps ensure the investigation is a single-variable exploration.
items.example: Weak aim: 'To determine whether the presence of an enzyme increases the rate of a chemical reaction.' Stronger aim: 'To determine whether the presence of invertase increases the rate of hydrolysis of sucrose by measuring the concentration of glucose produced using glucose test strips.'

items.title: I can write a hypothesis that is supported by scientific theory
items.what: A hypothesis is a specific, testable prediction that states what will happen to the dependent variable when the independent variable is changed, with a scientific reason drawn from relevant theory.
items.why: A hypothesis grounded in theory demonstrates understanding of the chemistry involved. If results contradict the hypothesis, the theory provides a basis for evaluating whether the experimental design or the prediction needs revision.
items.example: Weak hypothesis: 'The enzyme will increase the rate of reaction.' Strong hypothesis: 'The presence of invertase will increase the rate of hydrolysis of sucrose, producing an increased concentration of glucose, because invertase catalyses the reaction by lowering its activation energy via an alternative reaction pathway.'

items.title: I can define repeatability and reproducibility and distinguish between them
items.what: Repeatability is the ability to obtain the same results when the same experiment is repeated in the same laboratory by the same operator under the same conditions. Reproducibility is when the same results are obtained by different operators using different equipment.
items.why: These two terms are frequently confused in VCE responses. Repeatability improves reliability within one lab context; reproducibility strengthens scientific confidence by showing results hold across different conditions and investigators.
items.example: A student repeats the invertase experiment three times in their own lab — this tests repeatability. If another student in a different school runs the same experiment and gets similar results, that demonstrates reproducibility.

items.title: I can identify health, safety and ethical considerations relevant to an investigation
items.what: Safety considerations include identifying hazardous substances and equipment, and specifying required personal protective equipment (PPE) such as lab coats, gloves and safety glasses. Ethical considerations address whether living organisms are used and how any potential harm is minimised or justified.
items.why: VCE investigations require explicit safety and ethics documentation. Failing to address these reduces the quality of a logbook entry and can also lead to unsafe laboratory practices.
items.example: For the invertase investigation: safety requires lab coat, gloves and safety glasses. For ethics: the invertase used was commercially manufactured yeast-derived enzyme, so no living plants or animals were harmed in obtaining it. This addresses the ethical consideration of using living organisms.

items.title: I can identify sources of bias and explain how to minimise them
items.what: Bias occurs when aspects of the experimental design or data collection method consistently favour a particular outcome. Bias can be minimised by using blind measurement techniques, calibrating instruments against known standards, and ensuring controlled variables are truly constant.
items.why: Unaddressed bias compromises the validity and accuracy of results. Identifying and mitigating bias is a sign of a well-designed investigation and is rewarded in VCE extended response marking.
items.example: In the invertase glucose test strip experiment, bias could arise if the researcher subjectively interprets colour comparisons. Calibrating the test strips against a series of known glucose standard solutions before use would reduce this bias.
